title: Analyzing San Diego Airbnb Prices and Profits
text:
Airbnb provides comprehensive datasets that allow us to analyze the market landscape in San Diego, California. We will leverage one of these datasets to determine whether investing in an Airbnb property represents a viable and lucrative business opportunity. To evaluate this, our analysis will focus on three core business questions:

What is the average annualized revenue by property type?
Which submarkets and regions yield the highest financial returns?
How do guest reviews and ratings correlate with listing income?

To contextualize our findings, it is helpful to first define the primary room types available on the platform:

Entire Home/Apartment: Guests have the whole place to themselves. This typically includes a private entrance, bedroom, bathroom, and kitchen, with no shared living spaces or host present during the stay.
Private Room: Guests have their own private bedroom to sleep in, but other areas of the property (such as the kitchen, living room, or bathroom) are shared with the host or other guests.
Shared Room: Guests sleep in a space that is shared with others. This could mean sharing a bedroom with multiple beds (like a hostel style setup) or sleeping in a common area like a living room futon or sectioned-off space.




When entering a short-term rental market, one of the first and most critical decisions is choosing the right property type. Does a higher volume of cheaper private rooms outperform a few high-value entire homes? Below, we explore the relationship between room types, their price distributions, and their ultimate earning potential in San Diego.

Show tableHide table




Code
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)  #simple table
library(kableExtra)

airbnb<-read_csv("listings.csv")

#REVENUE (ROOM TYPE)
revenue<-airbnb %>% 
  mutate(price=as.numeric(str_remove_all(price, "[\\$,]"))) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(price), price<=5000, room_type!="Hotel room", !is.na(availability_365))%>% 
  group_by(room_type) %>% 
  summarize(number_of_proper = n(), avg_price= round(mean(price),2), risk_price= round(sd(price),2), year_occupancy=365-mean(availability_365), perc_occupancy= round(year_occupancy/365*100,2),proj_revenue= avg_price*year_occupancy, .groups = "drop") %>%   
  transmute("Category"=room_type,"Properties"=number_of_proper, " Service Occupancy"= round(year_occupancy,0),"Rate Occupancy by Year"=perc_occupancy,"Price (AVG)"=avg_price, "Price Variance"=risk_price, "Total Revenue"=round(proj_revenue,2))

my_styled_title <- "<span style='color: #000080; font-size: 18px; font-weight: bold;'>Summary Analysis by Room Type</span>"

kable(revenue, caption = my_styled_title, source = "Table1") %>%  
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "bordered") %>% 
  row_spec(row=0, bold = TRUE)

Code
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(scales)

library(sf) #points in data
library(tigris) #boundaries in map

library(DT) #better tables
library(htmltools) #custom dt table
library(knitr) #simple table
library(kableExtra)

airbnb<-read_csv("listings.csv")
#count prices
aprice<-airbnb %>% 
  mutate(price=as.numeric(str_remove_all(price, "[\\$,]"))) %>%  
  filter(!is.na(price), room_type!="Hotel room",price<=5000)%>% 
  group_by(room_type,price) %>% 
  summarise(count=n(), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  select(room_type, price, count) 

#donut chart
count_room<-airbnb %>%
  mutate(price=as.numeric(str_remove_all(price, "[\\$,]"))) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(price), price<=5000, room_type!="Hotel room", !is.na(availability_365),!is.na(estimated_revenue_l365d))%>% 
  group_by(room_type) %>% 
  summarize(number_of_proper = n(), margin_of_market=round(n()/11220*100,2), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  transmute("Category"=room_type,"Properties"=number_of_proper, "Market Occupancy"= margin_of_market)
 
#REVENUE (ROOM TYPE)
revenue<-airbnb %>% 
  mutate(price=as.numeric(str_remove_all(price, "[\\$,]"))) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(price), price<=5000, room_type!="Hotel room", !is.na(availability_365))%>% 
  group_by(room_type) %>% 
  summarize(number_of_proper = n(), avg_price= round(mean(price),2), risk_price= round(sd(price),2), year_occupancy=365-mean(availability_365), perc_occupancy= round(year_occupancy/365*100,2),proj_revenue= avg_price*year_occupancy, .groups = "drop") %>%   
  transmute("Category"=room_type,"Properties"=number_of_proper, " Service Occupancy"= round(year_occupancy,0),"Year Occupancy (%)"=perc_occupancy,"Price (AVG)"=avg_price, "Price Variance"=risk_price, "Total Revenue"=round(proj_revenue,2))

infoprice<-revenue %>% 
  select("Category", `Price (AVG)`, `Price Variance`, `Total Revenue`)



# DONUT - MARKET OCCUPANCY

hsize<-4
count_room<-count_room %>% 
  mutate(x=hsize)

ggplot(count_room, aes(x = hsize, y = `Market Occupancy`, fill = Category)) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = hsize + 1.5,# Pushes the text outward the donut ring
      label=paste0(`Market Occupancy`,"%")# Adds the % symbol to the values
    ),position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),#Centers the text of each slice
    size = 3.5,       # Adjust text size
    color = "black") +           # Text color
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.2, hsize + 1.5))+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0570B0", "#74A9CF", "#D0D1E6")) +
  labs(title="Market Share", subtitle="The biggest property counts comes from\n renting an Entire Home/Apartment", x=NULL, y=NULL)+
  theme_void()+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(color = "#000080", face="bold", size=14),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10, unit = "pt"), #margin - space around in and out graph
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", 
      color = "black",   # border around graph
      linewidth = 1        # thickness of the border line
    ))








Figure 1






There is a high supply in properties that are Entire apartments and Private rooms. The lowest one comes from the shared rooms. However, they also have the greatest occupancy in the market without having many properties compared to the others. Almost half of the year is reserved on shared rooms by the average customer.


All prices are calculated on a per-night basis. The following graph and table illustrates the frequency of specific price points across different property types:

This suggests that hosts prioritize keeping their properties affordable and accessible to maximize demand and overall profitability.

Figure 3







Looking thought the average price data between room types, we can see that there is a clear pricing hierarchy across property types, with entire homes commanding the highest rates, followed by private and shared rooms. Analysis of the average price data reveals a distinct pricing hierarchy across property types, following the pattern: Shared Room < Private Room < Entire Apartment/Home. Each tier roughly doubles in price (a +200% increase) compared to the previous one.
While this data highlights clear revenue potential, price distributions in the entire home/apartment and private room categories show wide variations. Constant market fluctuations make these higher-tier properties riskier to invest in. In contrast, shared rooms exhibit the most stable pricing within their category, offering a lower-risk profile.

Entire apartments generate the highest average revenue for investors in the San Diego, CA Airbnb market, while shared rooms yield the lowest returns. Hosts can identify excellent investment opportunities that align directly with their personal goals.


Looking through all these facts, there are two ways to make a good investment:

To earn a great revenue, the best investment would be to rent an entire apartment or Private room (Figure 4). These ones also come with higher market risk.
To make some extra money, you could rent out only a portion of your property. Since the demand for shared rooms is higher, there is greater stability and predictability in receiving income (Table 1).




Several Neighborhoods around San Diego, California, have different kinds of amenities, location advantage, and deals. what make each different is their success with their respect market.

WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

Luxury neighborhoods present growth opportunities, where expanding the number of high-quality listings could capitalize on strong revenue potential.
Investors should prioritize neighborhoods that balance revenue, demand, and market maturity, rather than focusing solely on the highest annual revenue.
Market size alone does not guarantee higher revenue.
Established markets offer lower investment risk, as their performance is supported by hundreds of active listings rather than a few exceptional properties.




The findings indicate that successful investments depend on balancing expected revenue, market competition, and investment risk:

Among all property types, entire homes/apartments generate the highest average annual revenue, making them the most attractive option for investors seeking maximum returns.
Private rooms provide a moderate balance between revenue and affordability.
shared rooms generate the lowest income but achieve the highest occupancy rates, offering a more stable and predictable source of revenue.
Higher-priced property types also experience greater price variability, resulting in increased investment risk.
Location is one of the strongest drivers of financial performance. Properties located near to the coast consistently outperform those farther inland.
Many high-performing neighborhoods combine strong demand with relatively limited competition, suggesting that high market demand can reduce revenue potential.
Service quality alone does not explain differences in revenue. Customer ratings remain consistently high across nearly all neighborhoods, with average review scores exceeding 4.8 out of 5.

title: Analyzing San Diego Airbnb Prices and Profits
text:
Airbnb provides comprehensive datasets that allow us to analyze the market landscape in San Diego, California. We will leverage one of these datasets to determine whether investing in an Airbnb property represents a viable and lucrative business opportunity. To evaluate this, our analysis will focus on three core business questions:

What is the average annualized revenue by property type?
Which submarkets and regions yield the highest financial returns?
How do guest reviews and ratings correlate with listing income?

To contextualize our findings, it is helpful to first define the primary room types available on the platform:

Entire Home/Apartment: Guests have the whole place to themselves. This typically includes a private entrance, bedroom, bathroom, and kitchen, with no shared living spaces or host present during the stay.
Private Room: Guests have their own private bedroom to sleep in, but other areas of the property (such as the kitchen, living room, or bathroom) are shared with the host or other guests.
Shared Room: Guests sleep in a space that is shared with others. This could mean sharing a bedroom with multiple beds (like a hostel style setup) or sleeping in a common area like a living room futon or sectioned-off space.




When entering a short-term rental market, one of the first and most critical decisions is choosing the right property type. Does a higher volume of cheaper private rooms outperform a few high-value entire homes? Below, we explore the relationship between room types, their price distributions, and their ultimate earning potential in San Diego.

WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

    "Loc. Rating"       = "r_location",
    "Annual Reviews"        = "Yreview_interactions",
    "Market Category"       = "market_category"
  ),
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10, 
    scrollX = TRUE,
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    # Shrinks font size directly in the rendered DataTable
    initComplete = JS(
      "function(settings, json) {",
      "$(this.api().table().node()).css({'font-size': '11px'});",
      "}"
    )
  ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  width = "100%",
  class = "compact stripe hover" # 'compact' tightens cell padding across all rows
) %>%
  formatCurrency(c("Est. Total Revenue"), "$") %>%
  formatRound(c("Accuracy Rating", "Cleanliness Rating", "Comm. Rating", "Loc. Rating"), 2)






Just looking at this table is possible to deduct some ideas of what is the customer preference based on the top 10 highest revenue of properties:

Guest satisfaction is consistently high across neighborhoods, with most ratings above 4.8, suggesting that differences in revenue are driven more by location and market demand than by service quality.
Luxury neighborhoods present growth opportunities, where expanding the number of high-quality listings could capitalize on strong revenue potential.
Investors should prioritize neighborhoods that balance revenue, demand, and market maturity, rather than focusing solely on the highest annual revenue.
Market size alone does not guarantee higher revenue.
Established markets offer lower investment risk, as their performance is supported by hundreds of active listings rather than a few exceptional properties.




The findings indicate that successful investments depend on balancing expected revenue, market competition, and investment risk:

Among all property types, entire homes/apartments generate the highest average annual revenue, making them the most attractive option for investors seeking maximum returns.
Private rooms provide a moderate balance between revenue and affordability.
shared rooms generate the lowest income but achieve the highest occupancy rates, offering a more stable and predictable source of revenue.
Higher-priced property types also experience greater price variability, resulting in increased investment risk.
Location is one of the strongest drivers of financial performance. Properties located near to the coast consistently outperform those farther inland.
Many high-performing neighborhoods combine strong demand with relatively limited competition, suggesting that high market demand can reduce revenue potential.
Service quality alone does not explain differences in revenue. Customer ratings remain consistently high across nearly all neighborhoods, with average review scores exceeding 4.8 out of 5.







Note on Methodology & Technical Implementation



The SQL queries and database integration pipeline used in this project were adapted and optimized with the assistance of Generative AI. All final data transformations, queries, and outputs were manually audited and verified for accuracy.

title: Analyzing San Diego Airbnb Prices and Profits
text:
Airbnb provides comprehensive datasets that allow us to analyze the market landscape in San Diego, California. We will leverage one of these datasets to determine whether investing in an Airbnb property represents a viable and lucrative business opportunity. To evaluate this, our analysis will focus on three core business questions:

What is the average annualized revenue by property type?
Which submarkets and regions yield the highest financial returns?
How do guest reviews and ratings correlate with listing income?

To contextualize our findings, it is helpful to first define the primary room types available on the platform:

Entire Home/Apartment: Guests have the whole place to themselves. This typically includes a private entrance, bedroom, bathroom, and kitchen, with no shared living spaces or host present during the stay.
Private Room: Guests have their own private bedroom to sleep in, but other areas of the property (such as the kitchen, living room, or bathroom) are shared with the host or other guests.
Shared Room: Guests sleep in a space that is shared with others. This could mean sharing a bedroom with multiple beds (like a hostel style setup) or sleeping in a common area like a living room futon or sectioned-off space.




When entering a short-term rental market, one of the first and most critical decisions is choosing the right property type. Does a higher volume of cheaper private rooms outperform a few high-value entire homes? Below, we explore the relationship between room types, their price distributions, and their ultimate earning potential in San Diego.

Show tableHide table

library(tidyverse)

  transmute("Category"=room_type,"Properties"=number_of_proper, " Service Occupancy"= round(year_occupancy,0),"Rate Occupancy by Year"=perc_occupancy,"Price (AVG)"=avg_price, "Price Variance"=risk_price, "Total Revenue"=round(proj_revenue,2))

While this data highlights clear revenue potential, price distributions in the entire home/apartment and private room categories show wide variations. Constant market fluctuations make these higher-tier properties riskier to invest in. In contrast, shared rooms exhibit the most stable pricing within their category, offering a lower-risk profile.

Looking through all these facts, there are two ways to make a good investment:

To earn a great revenue, the best investment would be to rent an entire apartment or Private room (Figure 4). These ones also come with higher market risk.
To make some extra money, you could rent out only a portion of your property. Since the demand for shared rooms is higher, there is greater stability and predictability in receiving income (Table 1).




Several Neighborhoods around San Diego, California, have different kinds of amenities, location advantage, and deals. what make each different is their success with their respect market.

These are neighborhoods experiencing strategic growth in listing volume and revenue. At first glance, the largest concentration of properties is around the beach (left side). As properties move further from the coast, the fewer properties. Finally, in order to get the best revenue per year, it is not required to be located in place strategically with many properties. Most properties with a great revenue are not in neighborhoods with many properties.

Shared rooms in the market offer an interesting insight. Most of the properties with the highest average revenue are located in the center of the city rather than near the coast. This is the opposite strategy from what other landlords use when renting other types of properties. Successful rentals are not bound by the rule of high supply in a neighborhood. A high number of properties does not mean better income performance in this type of property.


From the whole analysis, these are some of the main insights:

Location plays a significant role in revenue. For the most part, properties near the coast generate better revenue for landlords compared to those in the center of the city.
Higher revenue properties do not commonly face high local competition, as areas with top revenue tend to have a smaller supply of rentals in the neighborhood.
Potential investors and renders need to analyze which scenario would be most beneficial to them, depending on their investment amount and property holdings.

WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

Just looking at this table is possible to deduct some ideas of what is the customer preference based on the top 10 highest revenue of properties:

Guest satisfaction is consistently high across neighborhoods, with most ratings above 4.8, suggesting that differences in revenue are driven more by location and market demand than by service quality.
Luxury neighborhoods present growth opportunities, where expanding the number of high-quality listings could capitalize on strong revenue potential.
Investors should prioritize neighborhoods that balance revenue, demand, and market maturity, rather than focusing solely on the highest annual revenue.
Market size alone does not guarantee higher revenue.
Established markets offer lower investment risk, as their performance is supported by hundreds of active listings rather than a few exceptional properties.




The findings indicate that successful investments depend on balancing expected revenue, market competition, and investment risk:

Among all property types, entire homes/apartments generate the highest average annual revenue, making them the most attractive option for investors seeking maximum returns.
Private rooms provide a moderate balance between revenue and affordability.
shared rooms generate the lowest income but achieve the highest occupancy rates, offering a more stable and predictable source of revenue.
Higher-priced property types also experience greater price variability, resulting in increased investment risk.
Location is one of the strongest drivers of financial performance. Properties located near to the coast consistently outperform those farther inland.
Many high-performing neighborhoods combine strong demand with relatively limited competition, suggesting that high market demand can reduce revenue potential.
Service quality alone does not explain differences in revenue. Customer ratings remain consistently high across nearly all neighborhoods, with average review scores exceeding 4.8 out of 5.

title: Analyzing San Diego Airbnb Prices and Profits
text:
Airbnb provides comprehensive datasets that allow us to analyze the market landscape in San Diego, California. We will leverage one of these datasets to determine whether investing in an Airbnb property represents a viable and lucrative business opportunity. To evaluate this, our analysis will focus on three core business questions:

What is the average annualized revenue by property type?
Which submarkets and regions yield the highest financial returns?
How do guest reviews and ratings correlate with listing income?

To contextualize our findings, it is helpful to first define the primary room types available on the platform:

Entire Home/Apartment: Guests have the whole place to themselves. This typically includes a private entrance, bedroom, bathroom, and kitchen, with no shared living spaces or host present during the stay.
Private Room: Guests have their own private bedroom to sleep in, but other areas of the property (such as the kitchen, living room, or bathroom) are shared with the host or other guests.
Shared Room: Guests sleep in a space that is shared with others. This could mean sharing a bedroom with multiple beds (like a hostel style setup) or sleeping in a common area like a living room futon or sectioned-off space.




When entering a short-term rental market, one of the first and most critical decisions is choosing the right property type. Does a higher volume of cheaper private rooms outperform a few high-value entire homes? Below, we explore the relationship between room types, their price distributions, and their ultimate earning potential in San Diego.

To earn a great revenue, the best investment would be to rent an entire apartment or Private room (Figure 4). These ones also come with higher market risk.

Revenue generation is centered around San Diego, with the most success in the coastal area. In contrast, the center of the city does not account for the most profitable areas, yielding an average revenue of $30k–$45k. The best recommendation for investors is to note that most neighborhoods with a high supply of apartments show lower revenue. The best investments in entire apartments are located where there is a low supply of properties.

Code
WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

Just looking at this table is possible to deduct some ideas of what is the customer preference based on the top 10 highest revenue of properties:

Guest satisfaction is consistently high across neighborhoods, with most ratings above 4.8, suggesting that differences in revenue are driven more by location and market demand than by service quality.
Luxury neighborhoods present growth opportunities, where expanding the number of high-quality listings could capitalize on strong revenue potential.
Investors should prioritize neighborhoods that balance revenue, demand, and market maturity, rather than focusing solely on the highest annual revenue.
Market size alone does not guarantee higher revenue.
Established markets offer lower investment risk, as their performance is supported by hundreds of active listings rather than a few exceptional properties.




The findings indicate that successful investments depend on balancing expected revenue, market competition, and investment risk:

Among all property types, entire homes/apartments generate the highest average annual revenue, making them the most attractive option for investors seeking maximum returns.
Private rooms provide a moderate balance between revenue and affordability.
shared rooms generate the lowest income but achieve the highest occupancy rates, offering a more stable and predictable source of revenue.
Higher-priced property types also experience greater price variability, resulting in increased investment risk.
Location is one of the strongest drivers of financial performance. Properties located near to the coast consistently outperform those farther inland.
Many high-performing neighborhoods combine strong demand with relatively limited competition, suggesting that high market demand can reduce revenue potential.
Service quality alone does not explain differences in revenue. Customer ratings remain consistently high across nearly all neighborhoods, with average review scores exceeding 4.8 out of 5.

title: Long-Term Pricing Behavior & Management Strategy in Rexburg Student Housing
text:
Purpose of the Research
This study, therefore, aims to investigate the direct relationship between a student’s housing price and the variety of prices respect managing. The main question to answer in this research is: Do different management companies change prices over the years in different ways?
This experiment is applying the following two statistical test:

Two Way Anova : Examine whether contract prices differ across management companies.
Multiple Linear Regression (Two-lines): Identify what firms are varying the price and have significant variance based on years and managerial.


Two way-AnovaMultiple Linear Regression



Hypothesis

Does price change over time, regardless of management firm? \[
  H_0: \text{ There is no overall effect of year on contract price.} \\
  H_a: \text{ Year has a significant effect on contract price.}
\]
Do management firms charge different average prices? \[
  H_0: \text{All management companies have the same mean price.}\\
  H_a: \text{At least one management company has a different mean price.}
\]
Do some management companies increase prices faster or slower than others? \[
  H_0: \text{The effect of year is the same for all management companies.}\\
  H_a: \text{At least one company has a different yearly trend.}
\]

The significance level for this study will be set at: \[
  α=0.05
\]


Analysis with Two-way Anova
To perform the analysis we compute the following Two-way ANOVA.

pm.aov <- aov(Mean_Contract_Price ~ Year + Management_Name+Year:Management_Name, data=pricemanagement)
summary(pm.aov) %>% pander()

Diagnostic Plots
The Two-Way ANOVA test is considered valid, despite a minor deviation from its perfect assumptions. The diagnostic plots indicate that the assumptions of multiple linear regression are reasonably met. The residuals vs fitted plot shows no strong curvature or heteroscedasticity, suggesting that the linear modeling approach is appropriate. The Q–Q plot shows only mild tail deviations, indicating that residuals are approximately normally distributed. Together, these results support the validity of the regression model for analyzing contract price trends across management firms and years.

plot(pm.aov, which=1:2, pch=16)










Statistical Analysis

Main effect of year \[
F(1, 838) = 19.74\\
p = 1.007e-05 (< .001) → \text{significant}
\]

Interpretation: Average contract prices do change over time across the entire market.

Effect of Management Company \[
F(10, 838) = 33.36\\
p = 9.19e-55→ \text{significant}
\]

Interpretation: Management companies have different pricing levels, meaning the firm in charge matters for how much residents pay.

Interaction effect \[
F(10, 838) = 0.8774\\
p = 0.5541 → \text{not significant}
\]

Interpretation: Management companies do not differ in how their prices change over time. All firms show similar year-to-year pricing trends.


Conclusion
Contract prices vary significantly across years and across management companies, but the pattern of price increase over time is consistent across all firms. Year affects prices, and firms differ in their average pricing levels, but no firm increases prices faster or slower than others.




Hypothesis
This analysis attempts to model the accumulation of price rent through the years in student’s housing management. Specifically, \[
\underbrace{Y_i}_{\text{Price of Rent}} =
\overbrace{\beta_0}^{\text{Intercept}} +
\overbrace{\beta_1}^{\substack{\text{Years}}}
\underbrace{X_{1i}}_{\text{Management}} +
{\beta_2}{X_{2i}} + {\beta_3}{X_{3i}}+{\beta_4}{X_{4i}}+{\beta_5}{X_{5i}}+...+{\beta_11}{X_{11i}}+\epsilon_i
\]
The hypotheses test is:
\[
  H_0: \beta_1 = 0\\
  H_0: \beta_1 \neq 0\\
  α=0.05
\]
H₀: Price changes over Year are the same for all management companies. H₁: At least one management company shows a different pattern of price change over Year.


Graphical and Statistical Analysis

Diagnostic PlotsGraphStatistical analysis



Residuals vs Fitted: The points are roughly centered around 0 without a clear pattern. There is no strong curve or funnel shape, which indicates that the linearity assumption is appropriate and the variance of the residuals is fairly constant (Acceptable).
Normal Q-Q plots: This plot compares the distribution of the residuals to a normal distribution. Most of the points fall within the confidence bands, with only mild deviations in the tails. This indicates that the residuals are approximately normal and acceptable for linear regression (Acceptable).
Residuals vs Order: This plot checks whether residuals change over time or follow a trend. The points appear randomly scattered with no visible pattern or direction. This means the residuals are independent and do not show time-based correlation or clustering (Acceptable).

# Y vakues

  geom_point(size=0.8, alpha=.6) +

# Background
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
# X values correction 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The year 2025 is showing the highest contract prices among most managerial apartments. The data from most companies reveals a consistent pattern of yearly price increases. Over the four-year period, we can observe that most contract prices are relatively close to each other.However, Hemming and Triton Investments appear to have a greater annual price increase compared to the others. The primary explanation for the continuous yearly price increase across all companies might be caused by economic inflation.
To perform the analysis we compute the following Multiple regression:

# Multiple regression
pm.lm <- lm(Mean_Contract_Price ~ Year * Management_Name, data = pricemanagement)
# prediction

# plot
ggplot(pricemanagement, aes(x = Year, color = Management_Name)) +
# dots
  geom_point(aes(y = Mean_Contract_Price), alpha = 0.5, size = 0.5) +
# lines
  geom_line(aes(y = pred, group = Management_Name),size = 1) +
# titles
  labs(title = "Multiple Linear Regression Trends by Management Firm", x = "Year", y = "Contract Price", color = "Management Companies") +
# thematic template
  theme_minimal()








The regression analysis shows that each student-housing management company follows its own pricing pattern over time. Some companies steadily increase their contract prices, while others stay more stable or even decrease slightly. This means the student-housing market is not the same across all firms—each company sets prices differently based on its own strategy, demand, and operations. Overall, the data suggests that students may face different price trends depending on which company manages their housing.

This suggests a catch-up strategy or accelerated price adjustments unique to this company.








Conclusion

However, in the case of Triton Investments, there is statistically significant evidence that it might not follow the yearly price increase.
Most management companies increase rent at the same speed, and their prices are not statistically different from each other. Only one company — Triton Investments — stands out. They start off cheaper, but their prices go up faster every year than anyone else. So, in general, managers are not causing big differences in price trends, but Triton is an exception.

  labs(title = "Multiple Linear Regression Trends by Management Firm", x = "Year", y = "Contract Price", color = "Management Companies") +
# thematic template
  theme_minimal()








The regression analysis shows that each student-housing management company follows its own pricing pattern over time. Some companies steadily increase their contract prices, while others stay more stable or even decrease slightly. This means the student-housing market is not the same across all firms—each company sets prices differently based on its own strategy, demand, and operations. Overall, the data suggests that students may face different price trends depending on which company manages their housing.


Statistical analysis
The estimated slope of this regression is 50525, which is significantly different from zero (p=05.966e-15). Follows is a complete table showing the summary of the full regression results.

Regression results indicate that the majority of management companies do not significantly differ from the baseline firm in either their average pricing levels or their year-over-year pricing trends. The only firm showing a statistically distinct pattern is Triton Investments. Triton charges significantly lower average contract prices (p = 0.044) but exhibits a significantly higher annual rate of price increase (p = 0.004) relative to the baseline firm. This suggests a catch-up strategy or accelerated price adjustments unique to this company.



Conclusion
The regression analysis shows that most firms are no statistically significant evidence that the majority of companies differ either in their average pricing levels or in their rate of yearly price increases. However, in the case of Triton Investments, there is statistically significant evidence that it might not follow the yearly price increase.
Most management companies increase rent at the same speed, and their prices are not statistically different from each other. Only one company — Triton Investments — stands out. They start off cheaper, but their prices go up faster every year than anyone else. So, in general, managers are not causing big differences in price trends, but Triton is an exception.
We can see that Triton Investments has more related evidence to grow a 136.7$ per year faster than other managements.

title: Long-Term Pricing Behavior & Management Strategy in Rexburg Student Housing
text:
Code
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(pander)
library(DT)
library(mosaic)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

pricemanagement<-read_csv("pricemanagement.csv")

title: Long-Term Pricing Behavior & Management Strategy in Rexburg Student Housing
text:
Background
Student housing prices in Rexburg, Idaho have been increasing through the years. This study will determine if the increase in prices is not connected to the decision of housing management or other external factors.

title: Long-Term Pricing Behavior & Management Strategy in Rexburg Student Housing
text:
Data Collection
This data set contains observations regarding the prices over years for different complex apartments. Here are some of the important changes made in this data set:

The prices are rounded by using the means of each apartment. They are also converted to whole numbers since the difference is not significant.
We filter the data with the semester of Winter and Spring since this semester are the ones that are vary with respect the prices.
The managements are also part of the data with their respective apartment id.


Hide DataShow Data







Code
datatable(pricemanagement)

title: Long-Term Pricing Behavior & Management Strategy in Rexburg Student Housing
text:
Purpose of the Research
This study, therefore, aims to investigate the direct relationship between a student’s housing price and the variety of prices respect managing. The main question to answer in this research is: Do different management companies change prices over the years in different ways?
This experiment is applying the following two statistical test:

Two Way Anova : Examine whether contract prices differ across management companies.
Multiple Linear Regression (Two-lines): Identify what firms are varying the price and have significant variance based on years and managerial.


Two way-AnovaMultiple Linear Regression



Hypothesis

Does price change over time, regardless of management firm? \[
  H_0: \text{ There is no overall effect of year on contract price.} \\
  H_a: \text{ Year has a significant effect on contract price.}
\]
Do management firms charge different average prices? \[
  H_0: \text{All management companies have the same mean price.}\\
  H_a: \text{At least one management company has a different mean price.}
\]
Do some management companies increase prices faster or slower than others over time? \[
  H_0: \text{The effect of year is the same for all management companies.}\\
  H_a: \text{At least one company has a different yearly trend.}
\]

The significance level for this study will be set at: \[
  α=0.05
\]


Analysis with Two-way Anova
To perform the analysis we compute the following Two-way ANOVA.


Code
pm.aov <- aov(Mean_Contract_Price ~ Year + Management_Name+Year:Management_Name, data=pricemanagement)
pander(summary(pm.aov))

Diagnostic Plots
The Two-Way ANOVA test is considered valid, despite a minor deviation from its perfect assumptions. The diagnostic plots indicate that the assumptions of multiple linear regression are reasonably met. Conclusion
Contract prices vary significantly across years and across management companies, but the pattern of price increase over time is consistent across all firms. Year affects prices, and firms differ in their average pricing levels, but no firm increases prices faster or slower than others.




Hypothesis
This analysis attempts to model the accumulation of price rent through the years in student’s housing management. Specifically, \[
\underbrace{Y_i}_{\text{Price of Rent}} =
\overbrace{\beta_0}^{\text{Intercept}} +
\overbrace{\beta_1}^{\substack{\text{Years}}}
\underbrace{X_{1i}}_{\text{Management}} +
{\beta_2}{X_{2i}} + {\beta_3}{X_{3i}}+{\beta_4}{X_{4i}}+{\beta_5}{X_{5i}}+...+{\beta_11}{X_{11i}}+\epsilon_i
\]
The hypotheses test is:
\[
  H_0: \beta_1 = 0\\
  H_0: \beta_1 \neq 0\\
  α=0.05
\]
H₀: Price changes over Year are the same for all management companies. H₁: At least one management company shows a different pattern of price change over Year.

Normal Q-Q plots: This plot compares the distribution of the residuals to a normal distribution. Most of the points fall within the confidence bands, with only mild deviations in the tails. This indicates that the residuals are approximately normal and acceptable for linear regression (Acceptable).
Residuals vs Order: This plot checks whether residuals change over time or follow a trend. The points appear randomly scattered with no visible pattern or direction. This means the residuals are independent and do not show time-based correlation or clustering (Acceptable).

The regression analysis shows that most firms are no statistically significant evidence that the majority of companies differ either in their average pricing levels or in their rate of yearly price increases. Most management companies increase rent at the same speed, and their prices are not statistically different from each other. Only one company — Triton Investments — stands out. title: Analyzing San Diego Airbnb Prices and Profits
text:
Airbnb provides comprehensive datasets that allow us to analyze the market landscape in San Diego, California. We will leverage one of these datasets to determine whether investing in an Airbnb property represents a viable and lucrative business opportunity. To evaluate this, our analysis will focus on three core business questions:

What is the average annualized revenue by property type?
Which submarkets and regions yield the highest financial returns?
How do guest reviews and ratings correlate with listing income?

To contextualize our findings, it is helpful to first define the primary room types available on the platform:

Entire Home/Apartment: Guests have the whole place to themselves. This typically includes a private entrance, bedroom, bathroom, and kitchen, with no shared living spaces or host present during the stay.
Private Room: Guests have their own private bedroom to sleep in, but other areas of the property (such as the kitchen, living room, or bathroom) are shared with the host or other guests.
Shared Room: Guests sleep in a space that is shared with others. This could mean sharing a bedroom with multiple beds (like a hostel style setup) or sleeping in a common area like a living room futon or sectioned-off space.




When entering a short-term rental market, one of the first and most critical decisions is choosing the right property type. Does a higher volume of cheaper private rooms outperform a few high-value entire homes? Below, we explore the relationship between room types, their price distributions, and their ultimate earning potential in San Diego.

To earn a great revenue, the best investment would be to rent an entire apartment or Private room (Figure 4). These ones also come with higher market risk.

WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

title: Analyzing San Diego Airbnb Prices and Profits
text:
Airbnb provides comprehensive datasets that allow us to analyze the market landscape in San Diego, California. We will leverage one of these datasets to determine whether investing in an Airbnb property represents a viable and lucrative business opportunity. To evaluate this, our analysis will focus on three core business questions:

What is the average annualized revenue by property type?
Which submarkets and regions yield the highest financial returns?
How do guest reviews and ratings correlate with listing income?

To contextualize our findings, it is helpful to first define the primary room types available on the platform:

Entire Home/Apartment: Guests have the whole place to themselves. This typically includes a private entrance, bedroom, bathroom, and kitchen, with no shared living spaces or host present during the stay.
Private Room: Guests have their own private bedroom to sleep in, but other areas of the property (such as the kitchen, living room, or bathroom) are shared with the host or other guests.
Shared Room: Guests sleep in a space that is shared with others. This could mean sharing a bedroom with multiple beds (like a hostel style setup) or sleeping in a common area like a living room futon or sectioned-off space.




When entering a short-term rental market, one of the first and most critical decisions is choosing the right property type. Does a higher volume of cheaper private rooms outperform a few high-value entire homes? Below, we explore the relationship between room types, their price distributions, and their ultimate earning potential in San Diego.

Figure 4






Entire apartments generate the highest average revenue for investors in the San Diego, CA Airbnb market, while shared rooms yield the lowest returns. Hosts can identify excellent investment opportunities that align directly with their personal goals.


Looking through all these facts, there are two ways to make a good investment:

To earn a great revenue, the best investment would be to rent an entire apartment or Private room (Figure 4). These ones also come with higher market risk.
To make some extra money, you could rent out only a portion of your property. Since the demand for shared rooms is higher, there is greater stability and predictability in receiving income (Table 1).




Several Neighborhoods around San Diego, California, have different kinds of amenities, location advantage, and deals. what make each different is their success with their respect market.

Code
WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

datatable(
  rlistings,
  colnames = c(
    "Neighborhood"          = "loc_neighborhood",
    "Units"                 = "num_units",
    "Est. Total Revenue"    = "total_revenue",
    "Avg Accommodates"      = "accommodates",
    "Accuracy Rating"       = "r_accuracy",
    "Cleanliness Rating"    = "r_clean",
    "Comm. Rating"          = "r_communication",
    "Loc. Rating"       = "r_location",
    "Annual Reviews"        = "Yreview_interactions",
    "Market Category"       = "market_category"
  ),
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10, 
    scrollX = TRUE,
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    # Shrinks font size directly in the rendered DataTable
    initComplete = JS(
      "function(settings, json) {",
      "$(this.api().table().node()).css({'font-size': '11px'});",
      "}"
    )
  ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  width = "100%",
  class = "compact stripe hover" # 'compact' tightens cell padding across all rows
) %>%
  formatCurrency(c("Est. Total Revenue"), "$") %>%
  formatRound(c("Accuracy Rating", "Cleanliness Rating", "Comm. Rating", "Loc. Rating"), 2)






Just looking at this table is possible to deduct some ideas of what is the customer preference based on the top 10 highest revenue of properties:

Guest satisfaction is consistently high across neighborhoods, with most ratings above 4.8, suggesting that differences in revenue are driven more by location and market demand than by service quality.
Luxury neighborhoods present growth opportunities, where expanding the number of high-quality listings could capitalize on strong revenue potential.
Investors should prioritize neighborhoods that balance revenue, demand, and market maturity, rather than focusing solely on the highest annual revenue.
Market size alone does not guarantee higher revenue.
Established markets offer lower investment risk, as their performance is supported by hundreds of active listings rather than a few exceptional properties.




The findings indicate that successful investments depend on balancing expected revenue, market competition, and investment risk:

Among all property types, entire homes/apartments generate the highest average annual revenue, making them the most attractive option for investors seeking maximum returns.
Private rooms provide a moderate balance between revenue and affordability.
shared rooms generate the lowest income but achieve the highest occupancy rates, offering a more stable and predictable source of revenue.
Higher-priced property types also experience greater price variability, resulting in increased investment risk.
Location is one of the strongest drivers of financial performance. Properties located near to the coast consistently outperform those farther inland.
Many high-performing neighborhoods combine strong demand with relatively limited competition, suggesting that high market demand can reduce revenue potential.
Service quality alone does not explain differences in revenue. Customer ratings remain consistently high across nearly all neighborhoods, with average review scores exceeding 4.8 out of 5.







Note on Methodology & Technical Implementation

WITH aggregated_listings AS (
    SELECT 
        neighbourhood_cleansed AS loc_neighborhood,
        COUNT(id) AS num_units,
        CAST(AVG(TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price,
        AVG(365 - availability_365) AS avg_occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(accommodates) AS DECIMAL(10,0)) AS accommodates,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_accuracy) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_accuracy,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_cleanliness) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_clean,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_communication) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_communication,
        CAST(AVG(review_scores_location) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS r_location,
        CAST((CAST(AVG(reviews_per_month) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * 12) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS Yreview_interactions,
    FROM listings 
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND TRIM(price) != '' -- Filter out empty strings
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type IS NOT NULL 
        -- Safe numeric comparison with TRY_CAST:
        AND TRY_CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 5000
    GROUP BY neighbourhood_cleansed
)

SELECT 
    loc_neighborhood,
    num_units,
    (avg_price * avg_occupancy) AS total_revenue,
    accommodates,
    r_accuracy,
    r_clean,
    r_communication,
    r_location,
    Yreview_interactions,
CASE
    -- Large established markets
    WHEN num_units >= 100
         AND total_revenue >= 40000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
         AND Yreview_interactions >= 15
    THEN 'Established High-Performing Market'

    -- Small sample but exceptional revenue
    WHEN num_units < 30
         AND total_revenue >= 60000
         AND r_location >= 4.85
    THEN 'Luxury / High Potential'

    -- Solid investment opportunity
    WHEN total_revenue >= 35000
         AND avg_occupancy >= 200
         AND r_location >= 4.80
    THEN 'Growing Opportunity'

    -- High ratings but limited demand
    WHEN r_location >= 4.90
         AND Yreview_interactions < 10
    THEN 'Quality Market - Low Demand'

        ELSE 'Moderate Market'
    END AS market_category
FROM aggregated_listings
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

FROM (
    SELECT
        room_type,
        COUNT(*) AS num_properties,
        CAST(AVG(365 - availability_365) AS INTEGER) AS occupancy,
        CAST(AVG(CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', ''), '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS avg_price_night,
        CAST(AVG(CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', ''), '') AS DECIMAL(10,2))) * AVG(365 - availability_365) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS est_year_revenue,
        CAST(AVG(estimated_revenue_l365d) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS last_year_revenue,
        CAST(STDDEV(estimated_revenue_l365d) AS DECIMAL(12,2)) AS volatility,
        (CAST(STDDEV(estimated_revenue_l365d) AS DECIMAL(12,2)) / NULLIF(CAST(AVG(estimated_revenue_l365d) AS DECIMAL(12,2)), 0)) AS coeficient_var
    FROM listings
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL
        AND availability_365 IS NOT NULL
        AND estimated_revenue_l365d IS NOT NULL
        AND room_type <> 'Hotel room'
        AND TRY_CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(price, '$', ''), ',', ''), '') AS DECIMAL(10,2)) <= 10000
    GROUP BY room_type
) AS summary
ORDER BY est_year_revenue DESC;
